feedback.nudge: Three tests per sequence: is $\sum|x_n|$ finite, is $\sum x_n^2$ finite, is $\sup|x_n|$ finite. Do all three for each sequence before matching anything, and the descriptions will have only one home each.

explanation:
## The three conditions, in order

For sequences, $\ell^1 \subset \ell^2 \subset \ell^\infty$, and both inclusions are strict.

- $\ell^1 \subset \ell^2$: if $\sum|x_n|$ converges then $|x_n| \le 1$ eventually, so $|x_n|^2 \le |x_n|$ from that point on and the second series is dominated by the first.
- $\ell^2 \subset \ell^\infty$: if $\sum x_n^2$ converges then $x_n^2 \to 0$, so the terms are bounded.

This is the opposite of the inclusion for function spaces on a finite measure space, where $L^\infty \subset L^2 \subset L^1$, and the reason is worth holding on to: a sequence has infinitely many terms of "size 1" each, so the danger is at infinity; a function on $[0,1]$ has total measure 1, so the danger is a spike.

## Sequence by sequence

| sequence | $\sum |x_n|$ | $\sum x_n^2$ | $\sup |x_n|$ | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $2^{-n}$ | $1$ | $1/3$ | $1/2$ | all three |
| $1/n$ | diverges | $\pi^2/6$ | $1$ | $\ell^2, \ell^\infty$ |
| $1/\sqrt n$ | diverges | diverges | $1$ | $\ell^\infty$ only |
| $1$ | diverges | diverges | $1$ | $\ell^\infty$ only |
| $n$ | diverges | diverges | $\infty$ | none |

The two that are in $\ell^\infty$ only get there for different reasons, which is why they have separate descriptions. For $1/\sqrt n$ the terms do tend to zero — it is the **rate** that is too slow, and $\sum 1/n$ diverging is exactly the statement that $x_n^2 = 1/n$ is not summable. For the constant sequence the terms do not tend to zero at all, so neither series had a chance.

## The impossible one

"In $\ell^1$ and $\ell^2$ but not $\ell^\infty$" describes nothing, because $\ell^1 \subset \ell^\infty$. If $\sum |x_n|$ converges then the terms tend to zero, and a sequence tending to zero is bounded. A description that sounds like the others and cannot be satisfied is worth having in front of you: the inclusions between these spaces are a fact to be used, not a list to be memorised, and this is the cheapest way to check you have them the right way round.
